provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation:
The native rule works like this. There is one full divider line (colour 6) on background 8, and bars of 1-3 cells cross it perpendicularly. Each bar's extent (its interval perpendicular to the line) is measured. The extents are sorted by length and handed back to the bar groups in order along the line, shortest first. The native order is left-to-right for a horizontal line. For the generator's transposed scenes, which have a vertical line, it is top-to-bottom.

The emitted program works directly in visible coordinates and has explicit branches for a horizontal divider (a row with no background cells) and a vertical divider (such a column). It does not rotate or transpose anything.

I traced the native ordering direction through each D4 transform. A horizontal visible line takes its shortest bar on the right when d4 is in {1,2,4,5}, otherwise on the left. A vertical visible line takes its shortest bar at the bottom when d4 is in {2,3,5,6}, otherwise at the top. Reversed cases assign the sorted extents to the groups in reverse spatial order.

Extents are absolute intervals in the perpendicular coordinate, so they need no mirroring. The background and line colours are the constants palette[8] and palette[6]. Bar groups are maximal runs of non-line colour along the divider, split wherever the colour changes. Each run's extent is found by scanning outward from the divider in the run's first cell. Old bar cells off the divider are cleared to the background, and the bars are then redrawn with their reassigned extents.
draft_notes.limitations: The program relies on the constructor's guarantees. Bars never reach the grid edge, which keeps the divider the only fully non-background row or column. Adjacent bars always differ in colour, and bar colours never equal the line or background colour. Equal-length extents are identical, so ties are unambiguous; a stable sort is used anyway. If no divider is found, the input is returned unchanged. The archived program also produces an intermediate canvas with the bars cleared; that canvas is not emitted here, and only the final grid is returned. I did not run any tests. The fixtures agree with the uniform rule, and I found no contradictions.
